proposal: Take two random binary linear codes of length 8 and dimension 4 whose weight enumerators and other simple counting invariants agree, and treat the pair as a difficult instance of code equivalence. Deciding whether they are permutation-equivalent should then call for a collective multi-copy quantum measurement on coset states of the symmetric group.
killer: Polynomial-time permutation-invariant data, such as dimensions of Schur (componentwise) squares and hulls of the code, its dual and its punctured or shortened subcodes as used in Sendrier's support-splitting algorithm, separate such pairs, and random codes are the easy case for these methods. At this length one can also simply try all 8! = 40320 coordinate permutations.
lesson: Run the standard classical invariant battery (Schur powers, hulls, puncture and shortening refinements, support splitting) on any code pair before calling it hard.

note: Killer is only that one batch of low-degree Betti-number invariants collided on a single Goppa instance; no argument for why, and the claim is about a classical invariant rather than a quantum route.

proposal: Train a deep, randomly initialized, universal parameterized quantum circuit by gradient descent on shot-estimated gradients to minimize generic non-convex cost functions from optimization and learning. Because such circuits can express any unitary, this should give a scalable speedup over classical optimizers.
killer: Expressive circuits that approach unitary 2-designs have barren plateaus: gradient variance scales like the inverse dimension of the circuit's dynamical Lie algebra, which is exponential in the qubit count for a universal ansatz, so each descent step needs exponentially many shots (McClean et al. 2018; Ragone et al. and Fontana et al. 2024). Ansatze with polynomial-dimensional Lie algebras avoid this yet are typically simulable classically by Lie-algebraic methods, and hardware noise also flattens gradients exponentially with depth.
lesson: Trainability and classical simulability pull in opposite directions for variational circuits, so a speedup claim must show both a non-vanishing gradient and a reason the trainable model resists classical simulation.
note: Record overstates: polynomial-DLA implies classical simulability is a conjecture with partial results, not a theorem, and 'mathematically invalid' is too strong; failure_mode 'readout' looks mislabeled (trainability).

proposal: Pairs of binary BCH-type cyclic codes of length 15 with designed distance 3, built from different defining sets and agreeing on weight enumerators and on weight statistics restricted to small coordinate tuples, serve as hard non-equivalent instances for testing quantum coset-state attacks on code equivalence.
killer: Defining sets that coincide after closure under squaring (cyclotomic cosets mod 15) give the same code, and defining sets related by multiplication by a unit a mod 15 give codes that are permutation-equivalent via the coordinate map i -> a*i. The colliding pairs are of exactly this kind, so they are equivalent, and length-15 codes can be canonicalized by brute force anyway.
lesson: Before treating cyclic codes as hard pairs, reduce their defining sets modulo cyclotomic closure and multiplier (decimation) equivalence.

proposal: To find a hidden subgroup of the symmetric group S_n (say n = 10) generated by one involution that is a partial matching of the points, prepare coset states, apply the quantum Fourier transform over S_n, and record only the irreducible-representation name; polynomially many such names should pin down the hidden involution.
killer: The probability of each label depends on the hidden subgroup only through character values, and characters are class functions, so all conjugate involutions (all matchings of a given size) give identical label statistics (Hallgren-Russell-Ta-Shma). Even telling such an involution apart from the trivial subgroup gives only an exponentially small bias for large-support involutions (Kempe-Shalev), so entangled multi-register measurements would be required.
lesson: Weak Fourier sampling cannot separate conjugate hidden subgroups, so a symmetric-group HSP route must specify a measurement inside the representation spaces, usually across many copies.

proposal: For the hidden subgroup problem on S_14 where the hidden subgroup is generated by one involution with no fixed points (the case arising from graph isomorphism), a few coset-state copies should suffice: measure irrep labels plus a low-rank projection inside each representation, and combine the evidence across a small constant number of copies.
killer: Hallgren, Moore, Roetteler, Russell and Sen proved that for this family any measurement acting jointly on o(n log n) coset states, including arbitrary single-register or few-register strong Fourier sampling, yields negligible information about the involution. A working route needs a highly entangled measurement across Theta(n log n) copies together with an efficient decoder, and none is known.
lesson: For symmetric-group HSPs tied to graph isomorphism, budget for entangled measurements on order n log n copies from the start, since few-copy statistics are provably blind.
note: Near-duplicate of COSET-DISTINGUISHABILITY-DEBT-S10-FIXED_POINT_FREE_INVOLUTION.

proposal: Binary self-dual codes of length 48 make attractive targets for a quantum hidden-subgroup attack on code equivalence: their hull is the whole code, which defeats Sendrier's support-splitting algorithm, so a coset-state approach on them should escape the Fourier-sampling obstruction known for rigid graph-isomorphism-type instances.
killer: A typical self-dual code of this length has trivial permutation automorphism group, and refining coordinates by the supports of codewords of weight at most 8 already certifies this. For rigid codes the equivalence reduction produces an order-two hidden subgroup of exactly the form met in graph isomorphism, where Hallgren et al. and Dinh-Moore-Russell show Fourier sampling needs entangled measurements over Omega(n log n) copies.
lesson: Certify the automorphism structure of a code instance before assuming it lies outside the known coset-state obstructions.

note: Depends on an internal construction (one-uniform-subset-query output, mask bits, source-conditioned cell bound) that cannot be stated self-containedly in three sentences; the extension is also marked review-pending.

proposal: Because the pretty-good measurement on polynomially many coset states identifies a hidden subgroup of S_n generated by a partial-matching involution with high probability (verified explicitly for n = 8), this information-theoretic result already amounts to an efficient quantum algorithm for that family.
killer: Polynomial-copy distinguishability holds for every finite-group HSP (Ettinger-Hoyer-Knill), so it says nothing about running time; the hard part is implementing the measurement. Here the PGM is defined over an ensemble of exponentially many conjugate involutions and has no known polynomial-size circuit, compressed description or efficient decoder.
lesson: Separate information-theoretic sample complexity from computational cost, and require an explicit polynomial-time measurement and decoder for any coset-state algorithm.

proposal: For the hidden-shift problem on a known nondegenerate quadratic form f over a finite field, given oracle access to g(x) = f(x + s), the quantum algorithm needs O(1) queries while classical agreement statistics between f and shifted copies of g stay flat on random samples; this query separation is offered as evidence of an exponential quantum speedup.
killer: Here f(x + s) - f(x) = B(x, s) + f(s), where B is the nondegenerate bilinear form polar to f, so the difference is affine in x and O(n) classical queries plus Gaussian elimination recover s in polynomial time. More generally, polynomially many samples determine s information-theoretically, so only a computational (decoding) lower bound could support a speedup, and here decoding is linear algebra.
lesson: Hidden-shift evidence needs a lower bound on classical computation, not just on classical queries or samples, and low-degree functions fail because their finite differences are linear.

proposal: Pairs of binary cyclic codes of length 21 that agree on weight enumerator and low-weight statistics give a family of hard code-equivalence instances on which to design coset-state measurements.
killer: The candidate pairs collapse under standard closures: defining sets related by cyclotomic closure, or by a multiplier (a unit a mod 21 acting on coordinates as i -> a*i), give identical or permutation-equivalent codes, and the matroids of minimum-weight codewords match, so the pairs are in fact equivalent. Codes this short are also handled by exhaustive canonicalization.
lesson: A candidate code-equivalence family must survive structural invariants, closure under multipliers and canonicalization before it is used for quantum measurement design.
note: Near-duplicate in spirit of BCH-CODE-SEARCH-BCH_M4_D3_9; reason_invalid is a terse list of control labels.
Internal query model (missing-sign subset phase queries, source labels, carrier operations) cannot be made self-contained; the bound's scope is also narrow and self-qualified.
Internal objects (naturally occupied collision-free orientation frames, Sellke-typical tensor-covering blocks) cannot be defined concisely for an outside expert.

proposal: A commuting operator built from the class algebra of S_n separates every Kronecker multiplicity block (the multiplicity spaces in tensor products of irreducible representations) exactly at n = 8 and n = 9, so phase estimation on it gives an efficient uniform transform resolving these multiplicity labels for all n.
killer: Two small sizes give no asymptotic control: the smallest raw eigenvalue gap at n = 9 is already below about 4e-4, and phase-estimation cost grows inversely with the gap after normalizing by the operator's block-encoding norm. Without an all-n bound on that normalized gap, plus circuits, outcome statistics and a decoder, the gap may shrink superpolynomially and the transform would be inefficient.
lesson: Before turning a finite spectral separation into a circuit claim, prove an all-n bound on the normalized gap or find the size where it collapses.

proposal: For density-one modular subset sum as it arises from the dihedral coset problem, LLL-reduce the solution lattice and decode with Babai's nearest-plane algorithm; since the true witness's rounding deviations grow with n and escape a one-step search tree on every tested size, every polynomial-time decoder that applies an affine map followed by rounding must have negligible chance of recovering the witness.
killer: The experiment covers one reduced basis and one nearest-plane branching rule on finite inputs; other bases, other rounding or list rules and other affine maps are untouched, and finite growth curves are not a theorem about the instance ensemble. A lower bound for the whole decoder class needs a proof over the instance ensemble or a reduction from general affine decoding to the tested procedure.
lesson: Use finite failure profiles of one decoder to design new decoders or to state a conjecture, never as a lower bound for a whole decoder class.

proposal: Implementing the optimal measurement for the dihedral hidden subgroup problem reduces to random modular subset sum at density about one (Bacon-Childs-van Dam); solve those instances with LLL or BKZ reduction followed by bounded-distance or nearest-plane list decoding, which should return the 0/1 witness with inverse-polynomial probability in polynomial time.
killer: At density one the relevant lattice has determinant about 2^n, so by the Gaussian heuristic a ball whose radius equals the witness norm contains roughly 2^(1.047n) lattice points, and the witness sits about four times beyond the unique-decoding radius lambda_1/2. Euclidean decoders return whichever points are closest, typically non-binary, so any polynomial-size candidate list contains the witness with probability 2^(-Omega(n)); this is why lattice attacks on subset sum work only below density about 0.94.
lesson: At density one the planted binary solution is not geometrically special in the Euclidean norm, so lattice methods need structure beyond closest-vector search.
note: Record's 'any polynomial-size list decoder' bound rests on the Gaussian heuristic, not a proof; conclusion is standard.
Too terse: the oracle is not described; the record only says it is an arbitrary secret-finding oracle with an N=3 simulation cap.

proposal: Prove exact inverse-polynomial normalized spectral gaps for a commuting multiplicity-resolving Hamiltonian on every nontrivial stable shape of S_n (Young diagrams with a long first row and a fixed remainder); this would by itself constitute an efficient algorithm for the nonabelian hidden subgroup problem on S_n.
killer: Gaps make only one ingredient, a phase-estimation step, efficient. An algorithm still needs coherent circuits for the Fourier, label and coupling-change transforms, a proof that polynomially many outcomes carry enough information about the hidden subgroup, an efficient decoder, and evidence that classical methods do not match it, and none of these is supplied.
lesson: List every component of a quantum algorithm (state preparation, transforms, measurement, sample complexity, decoding, classical comparison) and check each before claiming a solution.

proposal: For a binary self-dual code of length 64, refine the coordinates by the supports of all codewords of weight at most 8; if some coordinate classes stay merged, conclude the code has nontrivial permutation automorphisms, so its equivalence problem falls outside the rigid case where coset-state Fourier sampling is known to fail.
killer: Unsplit classes under a bounded-weight refinement certify no automorphism, since refinement gives only a necessary condition, much as color refinement cannot certify graph automorphisms. For the code in question, using every codeword up to weight 10 splits each coordinate into a singleton, so it is rigid and lands in the order-two graph-isomorphism-type case covered by the Hallgren et al. obstruction.
lesson: Treat a bounded-weight refinement that leaves classes merged as inconclusive, and raise the weight bound or compute automorphisms exactly before claiming non-rigidity.

proposal: Extend quantum Fourier sampling to the non-compact Lie group SL(2, R): prepare coset states of a hidden discrete Fuchsian subgroup, Fourier transform onto the unitary dual (principal and discrete series), and measure representation labels and matrix entries, which should identify the hidden subgroup in polynomial time.
killer: Measured representation labels depend only on characters, which are class functions, so they cannot tell conjugate Fuchsian subgroups apart. The remaining information sits inside infinite-dimensional representations with a continuous Plancherel measure, where there is no normalizable coset state or finite measurement basis, and multi-copy measurements would need continuous recoupling coefficients with no known efficient discretized circuit; the problem is not even well posed without a finite-precision model of group elements.
lesson: Before extending Fourier sampling to a continuous non-compact group, fix a finite-precision encoding and check that the measured data are not conjugation-invariant.
note: Record overstates: conjugation invariance of weak Fourier data follows from characters being class functions, not from the Selberg trace formula; 'cannot be synthesized by discrete circuits' is unproven; '0.000 bits' is spurious precision.

proposal: In the dihedral coset approach, combine m single-qubit coset states with public random labels k_j into the state sum over subsets S of exp(2 pi i d k(S)/N)|S>, where k(S) is the subset sum mod N and d is the hidden shift. Then measure one public rank-one or polynomial-rank projection computed from the labels, chosen to forget which subset occurred while keeping the phase that encodes d.
killer: Averaged over the hidden shift, this state has eigenvalues equal to subset-sum multiplicities divided by 2^m, so it is bounded by c_max/2^m times the identity, with c_max the largest multiplicity. Any effect E fixed without knowledge of d therefore fires with average probability at most Tr(E) c_max/2^m, which is exponentially small for polynomial trace when m = Theta(n) and the labels are random.
lesson: A fixed low-rank measurement on an exponentially large, nearly maximally mixed register captures an exponentially small fraction of the state, so useful readouts must be full-rank with many outcomes.

note: Internal bridge construction (common-history overlap, coherent partial-solver bridge); killer is only an unproved all-n obligation, too abstract to state self-containedly.

proposal: Hallgren et al. proved that identifying a hidden fixed-point-free involution in S_n from coset states requires measurements entangled across Omega(n log n) copies; therefore the coset-state route to graph isomorphism cannot give a polynomial-time quantum algorithm.
killer: A copy count of order n log n is polynomial, so the bound only rules out measurements on fewer copies at a time, such as single-copy or constant-copy Fourier sampling. An efficient entangled measurement on that many copies is not excluded, and whether one exists is open.
lesson: Read a copy-complexity lower bound as a resource requirement and check whether it is polynomial before treating it as a no-go.

proposal: The explicit construction that resolved multiplicity spaces at n = 9, which stores each needed group-algebra element of S_n as a dense coefficient vector over all n! permutations and contracts these vectors directly, can be carried unchanged to n = 10 and beyond to continue the finite verification ladder.
killer: Memory and time grow with n!: at n = 10 a single degree-five support already needs 12630 rows of length 10! = 3628800, about 92 GB, while only multiplicity three has been contracted and target multiplicities reach 117. Factorial storage makes the approach infeasible within one or two more sizes.
lesson: Replace explicit group-indexed storage with representation-theoretic or class-algebra recurrences before scaling symmetric-group computations.

proposal: Use the hidden-shift problem for a noisy cubic chirp, g(x) = f(x + s) with f(x) = exp(2 pi i x^3/p) plus masking and noise added by the instance generator, as evidence of a natural quantum advantage, since it resists several standard classical baselines.
killer: Without the added noise and masking a shifted cubic is classically easy: (x + s)^3 has x^2-coefficient 3s, so a few queries and interpolation reveal s. The classical hardness therefore comes entirely from the hash, mask and noise that the generator injects, which makes the family an artificial pseudorandom construction rather than a natural structured problem.
lesson: Audit hidden-shift families for injected pseudorandomness, and check that the noise-free structured core is not classically easy, before counting them as evidence.

proposal: For random modular subset-sum instances at density one there are exponentially many short integer relations among the weights, so the 0/1 solutions must cluster at small Hamming distance from one another; hence no decoder that recovers a witness by affine rounding from a lattice basis can single out the planted solution.
killer: Short integer relations are generally not differences of two 0/1 solutions, since adding one to a 0/1 vector usually leaves {0,1}^n. Under the uniform planted model the other solutions behave like random binary vectors, so the chance that two valid witnesses lie within any fixed Hamming radius below n/2 is exponentially small; the claimed clustering is false and the no-go does not follow.
lesson: Distinguish lattice geometry from Boolean solution geometry: short lattice vectors need not connect valid binary witnesses.

proposal: Pick two binary Goppa codes of length 48 over GF(2^6) with Goppa polynomials of degree 3 that share parameters and weight enumerator; such a pair is a hard code-equivalence instance beyond classical invariants and a suitable test bed for nonabelian coset-state measurements.
killer: Polynomial-time permutation invariants already separate the pair: dimensions of Schur squares and hulls of the codes and their shortenings, or incidence statistics of low-weight words in the duals, differ, so a classical algorithm certifies non-equivalence quickly. Goppa codes carry algebraic structure (alternant form, recoverable support) that classical methods exploit.
lesson: Run Schur-product, hull, dual weight-incidence and support-recovery tests before using algebraic codes as hard instances.

proposal: For hidden fixed-point-free involutions in S_16, the case relevant to graph isomorphism, compute the copy number at which the optimal (pretty-good) collective measurement succeeds; since that threshold is polynomial, an efficient coset-state algorithm for this family follows.
killer: A polynomial copy threshold is guaranteed for every finite group by Ettinger-Hoyer-Knill and says nothing about running time. The PGM acts on Theta(n log n) entangled copies over an ensemble of (n-1)!! conjugate involutions, and no polynomial-size implementation or decoder for it is known; building one is exactly the open problem.
lesson: Treat a distinguishability threshold as a lower bound on resources, never as an algorithm.
note: Near-duplicate of COSET-PGM-CAPACITY-DEBT-S8-PARTIAL_MATCHING.

proposal: Coherently computing the multiplicity label in one fixed coupling order and one family of irreducible components of a multi-copy tensor product of S_n representations gives the full recoupling (Racah) transform needed for collective coset-state measurements, and thus a decoder for the hidden involution.
killer: A label in one coupling basis does not move between coupling trees, so it does not implement the unitary relating different coupling orders (the Racah coefficients); it acts on one family of sectors only, and nothing maps its outcomes to the hidden involution. A decoder needs transforms between overlapping couplings, their transition statistics, and a proof that the outcomes determine the hidden subgroup.
lesson: Distinguish measuring in one coupling basis from implementing the change between couplings, and never equate either with a decoder.

proposal: Attach reversible labels to q query-addressed local positive-semidefinite kernel blocks and combine them by exact Schur-complement recursion into one global endpoint quantity, so that arbitrary collections of addressed local kernels can be aggregated into the endpoint with polylog(q) quantum queries.
killer: Such a compiler would compute OR on q bits: let every block be zero except possibly one marked block equal to a fixed unit-norm kernel, so the aggregate equals 1 + OR(x) with a constant gap in endpoint probability, condition number one and constant mass. The BBBV lower bound then forces Omega(sqrt(q)) queries, ruling out polylog(q) for generic addressed aggregation.
lesson: Test any generic aggregation primitive against embedded search or OR instances, since their query lower bounds rule out polylogarithmic cost.

proposal: Two binary self-dual codes of length 16 and dimension 8, generated independently at random and sharing a weight enumerator, form a non-equivalent pair that is hard for classical code-equivalence algorithms and suitable as a coset-state benchmark.
killer: Up to equivalence there are only seven self-dual binary codes at that length, so independent draws are often equivalent; for this pair, bases can be chosen so that the two generator matrices have the same multiset of columns, an explicit GL(8,2)-plus-permutation equivalence witness. The pair is equivalent, not hard.
lesson: Check small-length instances against known classifications and explicit column-multiset witnesses before calling them inequivalent.

proposal: In S_10, identify a hidden subgroup of order two generated by an involution without fixed points from coset states by taking two or three copies, measuring each in a Fourier basis, and fitting the observed representation labels and row indices to a low-rank model of the hidden involution.
killer: For hidden fixed-point-free involutions in S_n, measurements on fewer than order n log n copies at once give negligible information (Moore-Russell-Schulman for single copies, Hallgren et al. for o(n log n) entangled copies), so a constant number of copies cannot work as n grows. A viable scheme must be a collective measurement over many copies with an explicit decoding cost.
lesson: Specify the full multi-copy measurement and its decoding cost for the whole ensemble of conjugate involutions before claiming a coset-state algorithm.
note: Near-duplicate of COSET-DISTINGUISHABILITY-DEBT-S14-FIXED_POINT_FREE_INVOLUTION.

proposal: Find a Hamiltonian in the commutant of the S_n action, supported on boundedly many tensor factors, whose spectrum is simple on each Kronecker multiplicity space for all sizes checked; phase-estimating it then yields a polynomial-time quantum transform onto multiplicity labels.
killer: Simple spectrum at finite sizes does not bound the eigenvalue gap as n grows. Phase estimation must resolve gaps of the LCU-normalized Hamiltonian, so its cost is the inverse of that normalized minimum gap, and without an inverse-polynomial lower bound on the relevant sectors the transform may need superpolynomial time.
lesson: Treat a finite simple spectrum as a hypothesis and prove gap scaling, or find an exactly solvable commutant algebra, before using it as a circuit primitive.

proposal: In a Kuperberg-style sieve for the dihedral hidden subgroup problem, sort qubits of the form |0> + exp(2 pi i k d/N)|1> into buckets by label k, and when estimating sample yield treat each combination of two qubits with nearby labels as producing their difference, so matched labels cancel deterministically.
killer: The CNOT-and-measure combination yields k1 - k2 or k1 + k2, each with probability 1/2, depending on a random measurement outcome, and only the difference branch helps collimation. Ignoring the discarded branch overstates the yield by a factor of two per combination, which compounds across sieve levels.
lesson: Charge every measurement branch and postselection step in a sieve's sample-yield exponent.

proposal: To estimate how well two hypotheses can be told apart from a classical-quantum state consisting of a classical source label and a quantum selector register, replace each hypothesis state by the product of its source-label marginal and its selector marginal, and bound the joint distinguishability by the marginal distances.
killer: Correlations between label and register can carry hypothesis information that neither marginal sees: two joint states with identical marginals, such as perfectly correlated versus perfectly anticorrelated bits, are perfectly distinguishable jointly and indistinguishable from marginals. In the tested case the joint trace distance (0.606) exceeds the sum of marginal distances (0.558), so the shortcut understates the signal.
lesson: Keep the full classical-quantum block structure when analyzing distinguishability, since product-of-marginals approximations can lose exactly the correlations that carry the signal.

proposal: Generate random binary self-dual codes with n = 16, keep pairs whose weight enumerators match and whose coordinate statistics look different, and use each such pair as a hard non-equivalent instance for testing quantum code-equivalence algorithms.
killer: Self-dual binary codes at that length fall into just seven equivalence classes, and for this pair bases can be chosen so that the two generator matrices have exactly the same multiset of columns, which exhibits a coordinate permutation mapping one code onto the other. The instance is equivalent and trivially certified so.
lesson: Remove any pair with a matching basis-normalized column multiset, and consult known classifications at small lengths, before building measurement experiments on it.
note: Near-duplicate of NEG-CODE-SELF-DUAL-GLOBAL-ORBIT-GLOBAL-ORBIT-SELF-DUAL-K8-00-01.

proposal: For the graph-isomorphism-type hidden subgroup problem on S_n with n = 12, where the hidden subgroup is generated by one fixed-point-free involution, run standard coset-state sampling and record only the irreducible-representation names returned by the quantum Fourier transform; their empirical frequencies should reveal the hidden involution.
killer: These frequencies are governed by characters, which take equal values on conjugate elements, and all involutions without fixed points are conjugate in S_n, so the frequencies carry no information about which one is hidden. Their deviation from trivial-subgroup frequencies is also exponentially small, which is why Hallgren et al. show entangled measurements on Omega(n log n) copies are needed.
lesson: Weak Fourier sampling is blind to conjugacy, so it is useless whenever the candidate hidden subgroups form a single conjugacy class.
note: Near-duplicate of WEAK-FOURIER-LABEL-BLOCKED-S10-PARTIAL_MATCHING.

proposal: For the dihedral coset problem with hidden d in Z_N, take independent single-copy samples (a random label k and a measured bit whose bias is cos(2 pi k d/N)) and form unbiased Monte Carlo estimators, linear in the samples, of the indicator that d lies in each of polynomially many coarse intervals; narrowing to the winning interval and recursing gives an efficient decoder.
killer: An unbiased estimator linear in single samples must reproduce the indicator of a set of size N/B from its Fourier coefficients over the random labels, and Parseval forces its second moment to be about N/B. With polynomially many buckets that is exponential, so exponentially many samples are needed, and keeping the sample count polynomial forces exponentially many buckets.
lesson: Linear Monte Carlo estimators inherit Parseval variance limits, so efficient phase localization needs nonlinear processing or a provably biased low-variance statistic.

note: Killer is only 'finite Schmidt ranks are not a theorem', and the record says a separate theorem already covers the declared random-source scope, so the claim is partly right and the item would be ambiguous.

proposal: Index erasure, the map from sum_x |x>|f(x)> to sum_x |f(x)> for an injective black-box f, needs Omega(sqrt(N)) quantum queries; since the dihedral subset-sum sieve must erase which subset produced each label, this lower bound shows that erasure step, and with it that route, cannot run in polynomial time.
killer: The lower bound holds for an arbitrary injective function available only as a black box. In the dihedral setting the labels are public and the map from subset to subset sum mod N is explicit, many-to-one and arithmetically structured, so it lies outside that model; transferring the bound would need a structure-preserving reduction, which is not given.
lesson: A black-box query lower bound applies to a structured problem only through an explicit reduction that preserves the structure.
